name: King Tubby's MCI console
originalPurpose: A twelve-into-four mixing desk built in the mid-1960s for ordinary studio work: balance the instruments, cut the record, go home.
whatActuallyHappened: When Byron Lee upgraded Dynamic Sounds to sixteen tracks in 1972, King Tubby bought the desk they were finished with. He then used it as something nobody builds a mixing desk to be. The faders became a performance: drop the vocal out entirely, bring it back for one word, push the snare into the echo and let it run. The desk's high-pass filter, a large knob that swept from 70 Hz up to 7.5 kHz, had a wider range at the bottom than most circuits of the period, and sweeping it live is the rising, hollowing-out sound on a great many records cut at his studio. The desk itself was built in the mid-1960s; 1972 is when it reached Tubby, which is the date that matters here and the one this record is placed on.
priceStory: Bought secondhand, because obsolete to a Kingston studio with new money was the only way this equipment was ever going to reach a Waterhouse engineer. The price is not recorded here. The economics are the point: the most consequential desk in Jamaican music was someone else's cast-off.
hook: A secondhand studio desk, played with both hands, which is where dub comes from.
blurb: A mixing desk is meant to be set up once so a song sounds right. Tubby treated it as something to perform on, live, onto a one-off disc. He would pull the singing out completely, leave the bass and drums, throw one word into an echo, then drop everything back in at once. The big filter knob on the right, with an unusually wide range, swept the sound thin and then full again. Dub's signature moves come from this particular desk: its faders, its send knobs and that filter. Tubby trained as an electronics repairman, and he modified what he owned, so the sound follows from his changes. He was not mixing a song, he was playing the desk.
